summary: Back in his own city, Jesus first pronounces a paralytic's sins forgiven and then heals him to make that invisible authority visible. He calls Matthew from a tax station and defends a table shared with sinners by quoting Hosea: God desires mercy, not sacrifice. Questions about fasting lead to images of bridegroom, cloth, and wine. Two intertwined healings, restored sight, and a contested exorcism end with compassion for shepherdless crowds and a call for workers.
whyItMatters: Matthew ties forgiveness, healing, table fellowship, mercy, faith, and mission into one movement. Religious objections keep asking who may speak, eat, touch, and restore; Jesus answers by acting with authority and by redefining righteousness around mercy.

context.author: Anonymous narrator abbreviating and grouping miracle and controversy traditions
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers familiar with Jewish Scripture, probably both Jewish and Gentile followers of Jesus; here, formed around mercy, faith, and mission
context.date: After AD 70 on most current views, often the 80s or 90s; earlier dates are defended
context.setting: His own city (Capernaum, 4:13) and surrounding Galilean towns
context.literaryForm: Miracle and controversy stories moving toward a mission summary

outline.heading: Forgiveness made visible in healing
outline.note: Men bring a paralyzed man on a bed; Jesus says his sins are forgiven, then tells him to take his mat home

outline.heading: Matthew's table and mercy over sacrifice
outline.note: Jesus says 'Follow me' to Matthew at the tax office; tax collectors and sinners eat with them; the sick need a physician

outline.heading: Bridegroom, cloth, and new wine
outline.note: Asked about fasting, Jesus speaks of the bridegroom, a cloth patch on an old garment, and new wine in old wineskins

outline.heading: A daughter and a hemorrhaging woman
outline.note: A ruler says his daughter just died; a woman bleeding twelve years touches his fringe; the girl arises

outline.heading: Sight, speech, controversy, and compassion
outline.note: Two blind men see and a mute man speaks; Pharisees blame the prince of demons; Jesus pities crowds like shepherdless sheep

keyVerses.text: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” (then he said to the paralytic), “Get up, and take up your mat, and go to your house.”
keyVerses.why: The visible command functions as evidence for the contested invisible pronouncement.

keyVerses.text: But you go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ for I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
keyVerses.why: Hosea's sentence becomes Matthew's interpretive rule for disputes about holiness and exclusion.

keyVerses.text: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.
keyVerses.why: Compassion, not recruitment strategy, generates the mission of chapter 10.

questions.question: Why does Jesus say ‘your sins are forgiven’ before addressing paralysis?
questions.answer: The story creates a test of authority. Forgiveness cannot be seen, while a body rising can; Jesus heals ‘that you may know’ the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive. The sequence does not teach that this man's disability was caused by a particular sin. It links two restorations without diagnosing blame.

questions.question: What does the crowd glorify God for giving ‘such authority to men’?
questions.answer: The plural can generalize from Jesus as a human figure or anticipate authority shared with disciples and community. Matthew does not stop to explain. At minimum, the crowd recognizes that divine authority is acting on earth through a person, a theme the Gospel will develop through sending, binding, forgiving, and the risen Jesus's universal authority.

questions.question: Why was eating with tax collectors scandalous?
questions.answer: Local tax workers served the revenue system through which Rome ruled, and the job was open to collecting more than was due (Luke 3:13); Matthew groups them with ‘sinners’ and Gentiles (9:11; 18:17). The Pharisees object to that table (9:11). Jesus's table does not declare injustice harmless: it enacts a physician's mission and calls people while refusing to make social respectability the admission requirement.

questions.question: What does ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ do to religious practice?
questions.answer: Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6, where covenant loyalty and knowledge of God outweigh ritual offered without fidelity. Hebrew hesed and Greek eleos carry mercy, kindness, and compassionate action. The saying does not abolish worship; it judges worship that becomes an excuse to withhold mercy from people.

questions.question: Do new cloth and new wine mean everything Jewish is old and Christianity replaces it?
questions.answer: No. Jesus and every speaker in the scene are Jewish, and Matthew affirms the Law and Prophets (5:17). The paired images warn that the bridegroom's presence cannot simply be squeezed into every inherited expectation or timing. They describe disruptive newness without labeling Judaism a discarded wineskin.

questions.question: Why does Jesus call the woman ‘daughter’ and say her faith saved her?
questions.answer: Sōzō can mean save, rescue, or heal; here the body is healed and a woman the law counted unclean (Leviticus 15:25) is publicly addressed as family. Her faith is not a substance that forces a miracle but trust expressed by approaching despite twelve years of bleeding. Jesus identifies the person, not the garment, as the relational center of the healing.

questions.question: What is the difference between the two reactions to the exorcism?
questions.answer: Crowds say nothing like this has appeared in Israel; Pharisees attribute the power to the ruler of demons. The same act produces wonder and hostile reinterpretation. Matthew is preparing the fuller dispute in chapter 12: evidence does not interpret itself when allegiance and authority are contested.

glossary.def: Jesus's characteristic self-designation, ranging from human vocation and suffering to the authority of Daniel's figure (Daniel 7:13; 26:64).
A local agent in the revenue system through which Rome ruled; Matthew groups them with ‘sinners’ and Gentiles (9:11; 18:17).
Compassionate, kind action; Matthew uses Hosea to make it a rule for interpreting holiness.
